assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks turned the magic-wavelength idea into clocks with fractional uncertainties near 1e-18, which lets us probe time and frequency, tests of fundamental constants and relativistic redshift over millimetre scales. This is atomic physics at its most precise, where theory and experiment agree quantitatively, and it opens genuinely new measurements rather than only an engineering improvement.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice concept and demonstrated the first strontium lattice clock; Ye's group pushed the stability and accuracy to the extreme and built the comparison and many-body clock work. Two laureates give a clean and fair configuration. The 2005 prize to Hall and Haensch (frequency combs) and the 2012 prize to Wineland and Haroche cover neighbouring ground but not this invention. Other contributors such as Lemonde and Pfau-type lattice work are not in the credited names.
assessment.maturity: Many independent laboratories (JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, PTB, NIST, SYRTE, NPL and others) have reproduced and surpassed the early results, so confirmation is strong and independent. Recognition is timely, since a redefinition of the second is under discussion.
uncertainties: Whether a clock prize would be judged too close to the 2005 and 2012 recognitions of precision spectroscopy and ion control.
My recollection of the detailed priority history between the lattice-clock proposals is from memory and not independently checked.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Aharonov-Bohm effect and the Berry phase show that potentials and geometry carry physical meaning in quantum mechanics, and they underlie much of modern topological and condensed-matter physics, atomic interferometry and molecular physics. This is exactly the kind of conceptually deep, unexpected insight about how nature works that I value, with applications nobody planned.
assessment.attribution: Aharonov and Bohm proposed the effect in 1959 (Bohm is deceased, so cannot share; Ehrenberg and Siday are earlier but also not available), and Berry discovered the geometric phase in 1984, with Aharonov-Anandan generalisation. The two-person list reflects a defensible but not fully complete picture of priority, since the story involves several people no longer living.
assessment.maturity: Both effects have been confirmed in many experiments for decades, including electron holography, mesoscopic rings, molecular conical intersections and neutron and optical interferometry. If anything the recognition is late rather than premature.
uncertainties: Combining two related but distinct discoveries in one prize may blur the citation.
Credit for the Aharonov-Bohm effect is complicated by the deceased co-originators, which weakens a clean attribution.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Ultracold atoms in optical lattices realised the Hubbard model with tunable parameters, with the superfluid to Mott insulator transition as the landmark, and opened quantum simulation of many-body physics, including single-site resolved quantum gas microscopes. This is a new way to study quantum matter and I find it scientifically compelling.
assessment.attribution: Zoller (with Jaksch, Cirac and others) provided the theoretical proposal; Greiner (with Hansch and Bloch) observed the Mott transition in 2002; Bloch led much of the subsequent development. Jaksch, Dalibard and Cirac also have strong claims and the five credited names cannot be reduced to three without leaving out significant contributors. The three-person choice is a compromise.
assessment.maturity: Reproduced and extended by dozens of groups for over two decades, with the Bose-Einstein condensation prize of 2001 as the natural precursor. Interpretation is stable, though the claim to solve open problems in condensed matter is still partly aspirational.
uncertainties: Allocation among Bloch, Greiner, Zoller, Cirac and Dalibard is genuinely contested and a three-person prize could be seen as unfair.
Overlap with candidates B023, B033 and B041 may split recognition.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Atom interferometry makes matter waves into precision instruments, enabling measurement of gravity, the gravitational constant, the fine-structure constant and inertial effects, and tests of the equivalence principle. It extends basic quantum mechanics of matter waves into precise metrology and has a direct link to the boundary between quantum and classical behaviour.
assessment.attribution: Pritchard's group demonstrated early atom interferometers, Bordé developed the theory of Ramsey-Bordé interferometry, and Kasevich (with Chu) realised light-pulse atom interferometry for gravimetry. Steven Chu was recognised in 1997 for cooling, which complicates how much of the credit remains. The three names offered form a reasonable configuration, but I cannot verify a precise priority ranking.
assessment.maturity: Strongly confirmed, with commercial gravimeters and large baseline instruments, though headline fundamental tests (equivalence principle, G) are still improving. Recognition is mature and not premature.
uncertainties: Overlap with the earlier 1997 and 2001 prizes may weaken the case.
Exact priority between Bordé, Pritchard, Kasevich, Chu and Chu's group is uncertain to me.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The prediction of the quantum spin Hall effect and Z2 topological insulators and its experimental realisation in HgTe is a major conceptual advance that created a whole field of topological matter. I defer to condensed-matter colleagues on relative standing, but the importance and originality look clear to me.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele made the decisive theoretical prediction, Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang predicted the HgTe quantum well realisation, and Molenkamp's group observed it in 2007. Zhang is deceased, which simplifies things, but Bernevig and Hughes are not in the credited names, and the three-name list gives a reasonable but incomplete picture. Moore, Balents, Fu and Hasan also made major contributions to the 3D case.
assessment.maturity: Extensively confirmed by many laboratories in 2D and 3D materials, and the interpretation is stable. The topological phases themselves recognised in 2016 are closely related, but topological insulators are a distinct discovery.
uncertainties: The line between this discovery and the 2016 prize on topological phases may be debated.
Distribution of credit between the 2D and 3D cases and among the many contributors is complicated.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Cirac-Zoller proposal for quantum gates with trapped ions and its experimental realisation by ion-trap groups is a foundational step in controlling individual quantum systems and quantum information processing. It builds on the 2012 prize to Wineland and Haroche, which weakens the novelty somewhat, but quantum control is rich fundamental physics.
assessment.attribution: The Cirac-Zoller theory is clearly decisive, and Blatt's group demonstrated the gate and much of the subsequent scaling. Wineland has already been recognised, and other experimentalists such as Monroe and Wineland's group made major contributions. Cirac and Zoller also appear in other candidates, so a prize configuration here would need to be coordinated with B009, B023 and B041.
assessment.maturity: Repeatedly confirmed in several laboratories, and used in commercial platforms. The practical impact of quantum computing is still developing, but the physics is mature.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2012 prize and with other candidates that credit Cirac and Zoller.
Whether Monroe should be included is not resolvable from the credited names.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Observation of fractional exchange statistics of quasiparticles in the fractional quantum Hall effect addresses a truly fundamental question about particle statistics in two dimensions. I find this appealing as a discovery that something genuinely new appears in nature, but I defer to condensed-matter colleagues on its standing.
assessment.attribution: Halperin made the early theoretical prediction of fractional statistics for Laughlin quasiparticles, with Arovas, Schrieffer and Wilczek; Fève's group (collider) and Manfra's group (interferometer) provided the key experiments. Nakamura and colleagues also reported results and are not among the credited names. The configuration is plausible but not obviously complete.
assessment.maturity: The first convincing experiments are from 2020 and have been supported by several independent set-ups, but the experimental record is still short and the interpretation of interferometer data has had some subtleties (e.g., Coulomb-dominated versus Aharonov-Bohm regimes). It may be somewhat premature.
uncertainties: Short experimental track record and limited independent replication.
Overlap with the theoretical anyon candidate B012 and unresolved credit for the original theory.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene revealed flat bands, correlated insulators and superconductivity in a tunable system, and launched the moire field. The discovery was surprising and the field is highly active, though I defer to colleagues in condensed matter.
assessment.attribution: Bistritzer and MacDonald predicted the flat bands in 2011, and Jarillo-Herrero's group discovered the correlated and superconducting phases in 2018. This gives a natural theory plus experiment pairing, though Cory Dean and others also made important contributions.
assessment.maturity: Reproduced by many groups, but the microscopic origin of the superconductivity and the correlated states is still debated and the field is young. Recognition may be somewhat early.
uncertainties: Pairing mechanism and nature of the correlated states remain unresolved.
Relative merit versus older and more established candidates.
